1. Create a citywide public awareness campaign teaching residents how to plan meals, store food, and use leftovers.
2. Offer free food-waste audits for households through municipal sustainability staff.
3. Distribute multilingual guides on refrigerator organization and safe use-by-date interpretation.
4. Partner with local radio and social media influencers to share weekly zero-waste recipes.
5. Provide subsidized countertop compost bins and curbside food-scrap collection.
6. Require grocery stores to post clear signage explaining the difference between best-by, sell-by, and use-by dates.
7. Encourage supermarkets to create discounted “imperfect produce” displays.
8. Establish a food recovery coordination office to connect donors with food banks.
9. Fund refrigerated vans to transport surplus food from retailers to shelters.
10. Launch a mobile app that alerts residents to nearby restaurants and stores selling surplus meals at reduced prices.
11. Require large food businesses to track and report food waste annually.
12. Offer tax credits or fee reductions to restaurants that donate edible surplus food.
13. Create standardized liability guidance so small businesses understand food donation protections.
14. Train restaurant staff on portion flexibility and waste-tracking systems.
15. Encourage restaurants to offer smaller portions and half-size menu options.
16. Require caterers to disclose surplus food availability for donation after events.
17. Set up a gleaning network that harvests excess fruit from residential trees for food pantries.
18. Map public fruit and nut trees and organize volunteer harvest days.
19. Support community gardens that grow food for local mutual-aid refrigerators.
20. Install community compost hubs in neighborhoods without yard space.
21. Partner with farmers markets to donate or compost unsold produce at closing time.
22. Provide market vendors with reusable crates that reduce bruising and spoilage.
23. Allow food scraps to be collected at farmers markets for composting or animal feed.
24. Create a city procurement policy favoring caterers with food-waste reduction plans.
25. Require city-funded events to donate surplus catered food or compost leftovers.
26. Ban large food events from sending edible food to landfill when a donation partner is available.
27. Introduce pay-as-you-throw trash pricing that makes food waste disposal more visible.
28. Provide separate organic waste collection for multifamily buildings.
29. Offer grants to apartment complexes that install food-scrap drop-off points.
30. Work with property managers to display food-waste reduction tips in laundry rooms and mailrooms.
31. Train school cafeteria staff to monitor plate waste and adjust menus accordingly.
32. Implement share tables in schools where students can leave unopened food for others.
33. Require school contracts to include edible food donation procedures.
34. Start school gardens that connect students to food cycles and composting.
35. Add food-waste lessons to city sustainability programs in classrooms.
36. Partner with universities to run food-waste hackathons and data challenges.
37. Support student-led campaigns for trayless dining and smaller servings.
38. Encourage hospitals and clinics to switch to pre-order meal systems.
39. Ask nursing homes and assisted-living facilities to use flexible meal ordering.
40. Create a citywide food donation hotline for institutions with surplus meals.
41. Build a regional composting facility to process food scraps locally.
42. Support anaerobic digestion projects that turn food waste into energy.
43. Develop a quality standard for municipal compost made from food scraps.
44. Sell or give finished compost to residents, parks, and urban farms.
45. Use food scraps from municipal collection for zoo or farm animal feed where safe.
46. Pilot insect-based bioconversion of food waste for animal feed or fertilizer.
47. Provide small grants to restaurants that install dehydrators or biodigesters.
48. Require new large developments to include food-waste storage and collection space.
49. Update zoning rules to allow composting and food recovery facilities in appropriate areas.
50. Create a public dashboard showing food waste diverted from landfill.
51. Fund a food waste baseline study to identify the largest sources and opportunities.
52. Use waste-sorting audits to understand what edible food is being discarded.
53. Adopt a city food-waste reduction target with annual progress reviews.
54. Hire a food systems coordinator to align waste reduction with hunger relief.
55. Include food-waste metrics in the city’s climate action plan.
56. Align food waste efforts with wastewater and landfill planning.
57. Establish a food-waste innovation fund for local startups and nonprofits.
58. Host pitch competitions for technologies that extend shelf life or redistribute food.
59. Pilot smart bins that measure food waste weights in commercial districts.
60. Use data from waste haulers to target education and collection improvements.
61. Encourage grocery stores to improve inventory forecasting to avoid overstocking perishables.
62. Support retailers in using dynamic pricing for items nearing expiration.
63. Promote first-in-first-out stocking practices in small corner stores.
64. Help corner stores install efficient refrigeration to reduce spoilage.
65. Provide training for food vendors on safe handling and date labeling.
66. Create a network of neighborhood free fridges with clear maintenance volunteers.
67. Support mutual aid groups that redistribute surplus prepared meals.
68. Coordinate with food banks to accept a wider range of fresh and prepared foods.
69. Offer safe-packaging guidance for donations of prepared foods.
70. Create emergency protocols for quickly donating food during power outages or closures.
71. Launch a “love your leftovers” restaurant certification program.
72. Recognize businesses that meet food-waste reduction standards with city awards.
73. Require city concession contracts to include waste prevention and donation clauses.
74. Train food-truck operators on inventory control and compostable packaging.
75. Encourage hotels to reduce buffet waste through made-to-order stations.
76. Work with convention centers to set food donation and composting plans for conferences.
77. Provide reusable containers to attendees at large public events to reduce leftovers.
78. Encourage event organizers to collect unopened bottled water and snacks for shelters.
79. Set up food scrap collection stations at festivals and street fairs.
80. Require food vendors at public parks to separate edible surplus from trash.
81. Create a repair-and-share program for kitchen tools that help residents preserve food.
82. Offer workshops on canning, pickling, freezing, and drying seasonal produce.
83. Teach residents how to make stocks, sauces, and snacks from food scraps.
84. Promote freezer-friendly meal prep challenges through libraries and community centers.
85. Provide library patrons with books and kits about food preservation and waste-free cooking.
86. Create seed-to-compost demonstrations at botanical gardens or extension offices.
87. Use community kitchens to process rescued food into shelf-stable products.
88. Support social enterprises that turn surplus produce into jams, sauces, or dried goods.
89. Partner with breweries and bakeries to use spent grains and other byproducts.
90. Encourage coffee shops to offer spent coffee grounds for compost or gardening.
91. Coordinate with waste haulers to offer food-scrap collection for small businesses.
92. Require commercial food generators above a threshold to separate organics.
93. Give haulers incentives to prioritize recycling and composting over landfill disposal.
94. Develop clear contamination rules for food-scrap collection to keep compost clean.
95. Use neighborhood ambassadors to help residents sort food waste correctly.
96. Run door-to-door outreach in high-density areas to improve participation.
97. Provide translation and accessibility support for all food-waste education.
98. Engage faith communities as donation and composting hubs.
99. Create partnerships with sports teams to promote food waste reduction at games.
100. Establish a permanent food waste advisory committee with residents, businesses, and nonprofits.

2. Provide discounted compost bins to residents.
3. Create public drop-off freezers for surplus edible food.
4. Partner with grocery stores to mark near-expiry items at discount.
5. Establish a food waste audit program for municipal buildings.
6. Require large food businesses to report surplus and waste data.
7. Fund a food rescue coordination platform connecting restaurants and shelters.
8. Offer tax incentives to businesses that donate edible food.
9. Train restaurant kitchens in waste-tracking and portion optimization.
10. Encourage supermarkets to sell imperfect produce at lower prices.
11. Install community composting hubs in neighborhoods and parks.
12. Use anaerobic digestion to convert food waste into biogas and fertilizer.
13. Require city events to use reusable or compostable serviceware and collect food scraps.
14. Launch a public awareness campaign on meal planning and storage.
15. Teach school children about food waste through hands-on cafeteria projects.
16. Create “share shelves” in libraries or community centers for nonperishable surplus food.
17. Support local apps that let residents share extra home-grown produce.
18. Mandate separate food waste bins for large institutions like hospitals and universities.
19. Provide grants for restaurants to adopt small-plate or flexible-menu models.
20. Set up gleaning networks to collect surplus crops from peri-urban farms.
21. Develop citywide date-label guidance to reduce confusion over sell-by dates.
22. Encourage bakeries to sell day-old goods through discount racks or partnerships.
23. Create a commercial composting facility to process food waste locally.
24. Require food vendors at farmers markets to donate or compost unsold items.
25. Offer free food safety training to shelters and community kitchens handling donations.
26. Require restaurants to offer reusable or recyclable containers for customer leftovers.
27. Promote “root-to-stem” cooking workshops at community centers.
28. Introduce pay-as-you-throw pricing that charges more for mixed trash than for compost.
29. Install smart scales in municipal cafeterias to measure plate waste.
30. Create a municipal food waste reduction target with annual progress reporting.
31. Encourage hotels to replace buffets with made-to-order options where feasible.
32. Provide mini-fridges and storage guides to small stores to keep produce fresh.
33. Launch a food donation hotline for businesses with occasional surplus.
34. Require event permits to include a food waste management plan.
35. Support mobile food rescue vehicles that collect small donations from multiple sites.
36. Create a city map of compost drop-off points, food pantries, and share fridges.
37. Give residents clear stickers for fridge organization to keep food visible.
38. Partner with local media to publish weekly recipes for surplus ingredients.
39. Require school cafeterias to offer share tables for unopened milk and fruit.
40. Train city inspectors to include waste prevention tips during restaurant inspections.
41. Introduce small compost containers for apartment buildings with limited space.
42. Distribute free airtight storage containers to households participating in food waste challenges.
43. Encourage caterers to offer half-portions and post-event donation options.
44. Create a food waste challenge with recognition for local restaurants.
45. Use city procurement to favor vendors with food waste reduction plans.
46. Create a city-sponsored competition for households to reduce food waste over thirty days.
47. Support farmers who use food scraps as animal feed where safe and legal.
48. Provide multilingual guides on storing fruits, vegetables, bread, and leftovers.
49. Establish a network of neighborhood fridges with maintenance volunteers.
50. Encourage grocery stores to donate prepared foods near closing to shelters.
51. Create “ugly produce” subscription boxes with local farmers and retailers.
52. Offer kitchen knife-skills classes to help people use more of each vegetable.
53. Install signage in public trash cans explaining food waste alternatives.
54. Require large residential buildings to provide food scrap collection space.
55. Partner with breweries and distilleries to use spent grains in baked goods or feed.
56. Support community gardens that compost local food scraps.
57. Develop a certification label for restaurants meeting food waste standards.
58. Create a city fund for cold-chain equipment needed by food rescue groups.
59. Encourage office cafeterias to switch to pre-order meals to reduce overproduction.
60. Train food bank volunteers in safe handling of rescued perishable food.
61. Launch a “freeze it” campaign encouraging residents to freeze bread, berries, and leftovers.
62. Encourage supermarkets to place soon-to-expire items near checkout for quick sale.
63. Provide small grants for schools to build compost learning gardens.
64. Require city-supported meals to prioritize donation, animal feed, and composting before disposal.
65. Create a digital dashboard showing citywide food waste diversion metrics.
66. Partner with faith groups to host community meals using rescued food.
67. Offer rebates for households adopting bokashi composting systems.
68. Encourage restaurants to list menu items designed to use trim and surplus ingredients.
69. Set up food scrap collection at farmers markets and transfer to compost sites.
70. Create a city ordinance banning large amounts of food waste from landfill disposal.
71. Provide training for food service managers on forecasting demand with sales data.
72. Establish a “last hour” marketplace for prepared foods nearing end of day.
73. Encourage hospitals to offer patient meal choice systems that reduce uneaten trays.
74. Create a food recovery liaison position within the city sustainability office.
75. Support mobile kitchens that turn surplus produce into soups and sauces.
76. Install clear labeling in public refrigerators indicating donation and pickup rules.
77. Require caterers to donate sealed leftovers when events end, if safe.
78. Encourage local farms to accept clean fruit and vegetable scraps for composting.
79. Launch a student competition to design food waste reduction projects for campuses.
80. Provide restaurants with smaller plates and containers for buffet or family-style service.
81. Develop a citywide “use first” bin program for fridges in schools and workplaces.
82. Encourage grocers to repurpose ripe fruit into smoothies or prepared items.
83. Train municipal staff to conduct waste sorting demonstrations at public events.
84. Create a shared cold storage warehouse for food rescue organizations.
85. Support food preservation workshops such as pickling, freezing, and canning.
86. Encourage wedding venues to include food donation clauses in contracts.
87. Provide grants for grocery stores to upgrade refrigeration and extend produce life.
88. Create a city-sponsored recipe booklet for common leftover ingredients.
89. Partner with delivery apps to let restaurants donate canceled or refused orders when safe.
90. Require food courts to separate organic waste from trash and recyclables.
91. Publish a fruit tree map and encourage residents to share harvests.
92. Offer subsidies for food businesses that install waste-tracking software.
93. Create a “good food pledge” for households, businesses, and institutions.
94. Encourage restaurants to provide leftover boxes without customers needing to ask.
95. Use compost generated from city food waste as free mulch for parks and gardens.
96. Establish a task force of chefs, farmers, and waste managers to guide policy.
97. Encourage supermarkets to train staff on stock rotation and proper display quantities.
98. Create a pilot for refrigerated lockers where residents can receive rescued food.
99. Require city food contracts to include plate-waste monitoring and reduction goals.
100. Celebrate annual food waste reduction awards to publicize successful local efforts.

lists.text:
1. A comprehensive city food waste audit can identify the biggest sources in homes, stores, institutions, and restaurants.  
2. A municipal food waste coordinator can align policies, partners, and funding across departments.  
3. Curbside organics collection can be expanded to all neighborhoods with clear guidance on acceptable materials.  
4. Pay-as-you-throw trash pricing can encourage residents to divert food scraps to composting or donation channels.  
5. The city can subsidize backyard compost bins and worm composting kits for households.  
6. Neighborhood compost drop-off sites can serve residents who lack curbside pickup.  
7. A public food-sharing app can connect households with surplus food to neighbors, shelters, or food pantries.  
8. Local grocery stores can adopt standardized date labels that distinguish safety dates from quality dates.  
9. Restaurants can offer smaller portions and clearly identify leftover-friendly menu items.  
10. A city-funded awareness campaign can teach residents how to store produce, plan meals, and use leftovers.  
11. Schools can implement offer-versus-serve meal programs so students take only what they will eat.  
12. School cafeterias can add share tables where unopened food can be taken by others.  
13. Universities and colleges can use trayless dining to reduce plate waste.  
14. Hospitals and senior centers can adjust portion sizes based on patient and resident preferences.  
15. Food banks can receive city support for cold storage and rapid distribution of perishable donations.  
16. A food rescue logistics network can use volunteers and vans to move surplus food from businesses to charities.  
17. Local farms can partner with retailers to accept imperfect produce for processing or animal feed.  
18. Farmers markets can sell cosmetically flawed fruits and vegetables at discounted prices.  
19. A gleaning program can collect surplus crops from urban farms and nearby growers.  
20. City procurement rules can require caterers to donate edible leftovers when contracts exceed a certain size.  
21. Municipal events can require vendors to follow food waste reduction plans.  
22. Food waste in city facilities can be tracked through regular weigh-ins and public reporting.  
23. Public kitchens can host workshops on preserving, pickling, freezing, and fermenting surplus food.  
24. Libraries can lend food preservation equipment such as dehydrators, canning kits, and vacuum sealers.  
25. Community refrigerators can be installed in accessible locations for safe sharing of perishable food.  
26. Local restaurants can join a surplus food marketplace that offers discounted end-of-day meals.  
27. Bakeries can partner with breweries or farms to turn stale bread into beer, croutons, breadcrumbs, or animal feed.  
28. Grocery stores can create dedicated sections for near-expiry items at reduced prices.  
29. Retail staff can be trained in first-expired-first-out stocking and careful produce handling.  
30. Supermarkets can donate damaged but edible packaged foods through liability-protected food rescue programs.  
31. The city can provide tax incentives or fee reductions to businesses that donate surplus food.  
32. A recognition program can certify restaurants and stores that meet food waste reduction standards.  
33. Food service contractors can be required to use forecasting tools to avoid overproduction.  
34. Buffets can switch to smaller pans and batch cooking based on real-time demand.  
35. Cafeterias can use plate waste audits to adjust menus and serving sizes.  
36. Hotels can reduce breakfast waste by offering made-to-order options and clear portion choices.  
37. Convention centers can require event organizers to plan food quantities using historical attendance data.  
38. Stadiums and arenas can donate unsold prepared food through pre-arranged food rescue agreements.  
39. Food trucks can use pre-ordering systems to better match supply and demand.  
40. Meal kit companies can be encouraged to use local surplus produce in their menus.  
41. A city-supported repair café can include appliance repair for refrigerators, freezers, and blenders to keep food usable.  
42. Utility programs can offer rebates for energy-efficient refrigerators that keep food fresh longer.  
43. Housing developers can design kitchens with better storage, freezer space, and visibility of food.  
44. Community gardens can grow preservation crops and host harvest-processing days.  
45. The city can fund mobile cold storage units for food rescue organizations.  
46. A centralized food donation platform can match businesses with charities based on food type, quantity, and pickup needs.  
47. Food safety guidelines for donations can be published in simple multilingual formats.  
48. Local health inspectors can include waste prevention tips during routine food establishment visits.  
49. The city can create a food waste reduction pledge for households with practical weekly goals.  
50. Faith communities can host food-saving clubs where members cook from surplus ingredients together.  
51. Youth groups can run competitions to create recipes from commonly wasted foods.  
52. Local media can feature weekly recipes using bread ends, vegetable trimmings, overripe fruit, and leftovers.  
53. Grocery stores can provide recipe cards near produce that highlight uses for blemished items.  
54. The city can sponsor a zero-waste cooking challenge among local restaurants.  
55. Neighborhood-level organics collection data can be published quarterly to identify areas needing targeted outreach.  
56. Waste haulers can provide residents with feedback reports on how much organics they diverted.  
57. A pilot anaerobic digestion facility can convert food scraps into energy and soil amendments.  
58. Local wastewater treatment plants can co-digest food waste to improve renewable energy production.  
59. The city can require large food generators above a threshold to separate edible food for donation and scraps for composting.  
60. Commercial food waste landfill restrictions can be paired with affordable diversion services.  
61. Compost produced from city food scraps can be used in urban farms, parks, and tree-planting programs.  
62. The city can support black soldier fly facilities that process food scraps into animal feed ingredients.  
63. Restaurants can use reusable containers for leftovers instead of single-use packaging that discourages taking food home.  
64. Takeout ordering platforms can let customers opt out of unwanted side items that often become food waste.  
65. Food delivery services can add features that suggest right-sized orders based on household size.  
66. City offices can adopt internal food-sharing shelves for unopened snacks and beverages.  
67. Workplaces can host lunch-and-learn sessions on meal planning and freezer use.  
68. Corporate cafeterias can use dynamic pricing to sell remaining meals near closing time.  
69. Retail chains can share anonymized waste data with the city to benchmark prevention efforts.  
70. A local innovation grant can fund startups developing shelf-life extension technologies for small retailers.  
71. The city can encourage corner stores to join cooperative purchasing to reduce spoilage from oversized orders.  
72. Small grocers can receive help installing better refrigeration and humidity controls.  
73. Food hubs can aggregate surplus produce for use in soups, sauces, frozen mixes, and baby food.  
74. A municipal kitchen incubator can help entrepreneurs turn surplus food into value-added products.  
75. The city can create a surplus produce contract with local processors during peak harvest season.  
76. Food scrap collection routes can be optimized to reduce contamination and missed pickups.  
77. Public signage in multiple languages can clarify what can and cannot be composted.  
78. The city can train volunteer food waste ambassadors to coach neighbors on simple prevention habits.  
79. Utility bills can include seasonal tips for storing food and reducing household waste.  
80. A city-sponsored reuse event can include demonstrations on reviving wilted vegetables and stale bread.  
81. Schools can partner with local farms to turn food scraps into compost for school gardens.  
82. School gardens can teach students about growing, harvesting, and eating whole foods.  
83. Cafeterias can pre-cut fruits and vegetables in ways that increase consumption and reduce peel waste.  
84. Food service bids can require vendors to include waste prevention, donation, and composting plans.  
85. Food vendors can be required to report waste quantities at large festivals and street fairs.  
86. Event organizers can collect edible leftovers through scheduled pickups with certified food rescue groups.  
87. A real-time dashboard can help city managers monitor organics collection tonnage and contamination rates.  
88. The city can use behavioral nudges such as smaller plates in public dining settings.  
89. Grocery stores can use shelf sensors and inventory analytics to reduce overstocking of perishables.  
90. Restaurants can train servers to ask about appetite levels before taking orders.  
91. A local food waste hotline can help residents and businesses find donation, composting, and recycling options.  
92. The city can publish a map of food donation points, compost sites, and community fridges.  
93. A seasonal storage guide can help residents extend the life of local fruits, vegetables, herbs, and grains.  
94. Neighborhood associations can host swap days for garden produce and pantry staples before they spoil.  
95. The city can collaborate with landlords to provide shared food waste bins in multi-family buildings.  
96. Property managers can receive toolkits for reducing food waste in apartment complexes.  
97. Transit ads can normalize asking for leftovers and smaller portions.  
98. The city can integrate food waste reduction into climate action and zero-waste planning.  
99. Annual awards can highlight households, schools, businesses, and nonprofits achieving measurable food waste reductions.  
100. A cross-sector food waste council can review progress each year and recommend new policies, partnerships, and funding.

1. Launch a citywide public education campaign on meal planning, storage, and leftovers.
2. Offer free workshops in community centers on preserving, freezing, and composting food.
3. Require grocery stores to separate unsold edible food for donation instead of disposal.
4. Create a municipal food rescue coordinator role to connect donors, volunteers, and shelters.
5. Provide tax incentives to restaurants that donate surplus meals to certified nonprofits.
6. Standardize a local “best by” education program to reduce confusion over date labels.
7. Fund a network of public compost drop-off sites in neighborhoods, parks, and farmers markets.
8. Introduce curbside organics collection for all residential households.
9. Subsidize countertop compost bins for apartments and small homes.
10. Partner with schools to teach students about food waste through hands-on cafeteria projects.
11. Establish a gleaning program that collects excess produce from urban gardens and nearby farms.
12. Create a mobile app that alerts residents to discounted near-expiry items at local stores.
13. Encourage supermarkets to sell “imperfect” fruits and vegetables at reduced prices.
14. Set up refrigerated community fridges where businesses and residents can share edible food.
15. Require city-funded events to use reusable serviceware and donate leftover catered food.
16. Develop a food waste audit program for restaurants to identify their biggest sources of waste.
17. Train chefs to design menus that use stems, peels, bones, and day-old ingredients.
18. Provide small grants to food businesses that install waste-tracking technology.
19. Establish a city policy that prioritizes waste prevention before composting or disposal.
20. Create a recognition program for businesses that achieve measurable food waste reductions.
21. Coordinate with food banks to expand cold-chain capacity for perishable donations.
22. Launch a volunteer driver network to transport small food donations quickly.
23. Require large institutions such as hospitals and universities to report food waste data annually.
24. Support a reusable container program for takeout meals to reduce packaging and plate waste.
25. Install signage in multiple languages explaining proper sorting of food scraps.
26. Encourage hotels to track buffet waste and adjust purchasing based on demand.
27. Create a city-sponsored recipe series using common surplus ingredients.
28. Fund school gardens that turn cafeteria scraps into compost for growing food.
29. Partner with local farms to use food scraps as animal feed where safe and legal.
30. Introduce pay-as-you-throw pricing to discourage disposal of mixed waste.
31. Offer rebates for residents who buy or build backyard compost systems.
32. Establish a food waste hotline or online portal for reporting unnecessary disposal.
33. Require city vendors at festivals to minimize single-use portions and surplus prep.
34. Encourage grocery stores to cut tray sizes for perishables to reduce overbuying.
35. Promote “first in, first out” practices in home kitchens through simple sticker kits.
36. Create a network of neighborhood repair cafés that also teach food preservation skills.
37. Support local entrepreneurs who make products from surplus food, such as jams or dried snacks.
38. Provide clear guidelines for safe food donation to reduce liability fears among businesses.
39. Create a public dashboard showing city progress on food waste reduction and diversion.
40. Require municipal cafeterias to use smaller plates and serve flexible portions.
41. Launch a zero-waste certification for restaurants based on prevention, donation, and composting.
42. Partner with faith groups to host community meals using rescued ingredients.
43. Establish a citywide challenge where households pledge to reduce food waste for a month.
44. Encourage farmers markets to sell day-end produce at discount or donate it.
45. Train market vendors to store produce properly to extend freshness.
46. Create a food recovery hub that aggregates surplus from multiple businesses.
47. Use city land for composting facilities that process local food scraps.
48. Provide composting education for property managers of multifamily housing.
49. Encourage landlords to include compost collection space in building waste areas.
50. Develop a toolkit for offices to reduce snack and coffee-room food waste.
51. Require new large developments to include space for food waste separation and storage.
52. Support a deposit program for reusable food containers at universities and downtown eateries.
53. Encourage caterers to offer smaller buffet trays and replenish them as needed.
54. Create a city procurement policy that requires event catering to include waste-reduction clauses.
55. Offer free software or templates to small grocers for inventory and expiration tracking.
56. Encourage stores to bundle near-expiry items into meal kits or discounted baskets.
57. Partner with local media to share stories of residents and businesses reducing food waste.
58. Integrate food waste prevention into climate action and sustainability plans.
59. Fund research with local colleges on the city’s food waste flows and best interventions.
60. Create a food donation liability guide based on national and local food safety laws.
61. Host seasonal preservation fairs focused on canning, pickling, drying, and freezing.
62. Require food service contractors in city buildings to meet waste reduction targets.
63. Encourage restaurants to offer half portions and smaller sides to reduce plate waste.
64. Create a “take what you need” shelf at libraries or community centers for nonperishable food.
65. Install smart scales in municipal kitchens to measure and reduce prep waste.
66. Provide training for food service workers on proper portioning and batch cooking.
67. Develop a city-approved list of compostable bags and liners to avoid contamination.
68. Encourage supermarkets to use dynamic pricing for items approaching their sell-by dates.
69. Promote freezer-friendly meal prep classes for seniors, students, and busy families.
70. Create a network of volunteer food waste ambassadors to coach households door-to-door.
71. Establish clear rules allowing urban farmers to collect food scraps from nearby businesses.
72. Require food waste education packets for new residents during move-in or utility registration.
73. Encourage cafés to train baristas to steam milk efficiently and offer smaller drink sizes.
74. Support pop-up dinners where chefs cook exclusively with rescued food.
75. Create a city challenge for schools to achieve the lowest per-student cafeteria waste.
76. Provide reusable crates for farmers and vendors to reduce damaged produce during transport.
77. Encourage grocery stores to donate bakery items from the previous day instead of discarding them.
78. Introduce compost collection at public parks, sports fields, and recreation centers.
79. Create a shared cold storage space for food rescue organizations.
80. Require large food businesses to train staff on waste separation and donation procedures.
81. Encourage households to keep a visible “eat me first” bin in the refrigerator.
82. Provide multilingual guides on safe storage times for common foods.
83. Support community kitchens that process surplus produce into meals for distribution.
84. Offer matching funds for neighborhood groups that start food-sharing or composting projects.
85. Create a city-sponsored award for innovative packaging that reduces spoilage.
86. Encourage restaurants to list menu items that use surplus ingredients.
87. Require city departments to coordinate food event permits with waste reduction requirements.
88. Partner with waste haulers to offer discounted organics pickup for food-heavy businesses.
89. Develop a standardized donation receipt system to simplify recordkeeping for food donors.
90. Encourage corner stores to stock smaller portions of fresh produce for nearby residents.
91. Launch a public art campaign using food waste visuals to change social norms.
92. Require food courts in municipal buildings to provide clearly marked compost and donation stations.
93. Support a local tool library that includes dehydrators, canners, and vacuum sealers.
94. Encourage wedding and event venues to include food donation plans in contracts.
95. Create a citywide inventory of refrigerated storage, trucks, and volunteers for food rescue.
96. Promote ugly produce smoothies, soups, and sauces in cafés and institutional kitchens.
97. Train city inspectors to advise businesses on food waste prevention during routine visits.
98. Encourage supermarkets to place clear storage tips near fresh produce and bakery sections.
99. Establish an annual food waste awareness week with events in schools, markets, and businesses.
100. Create a permanent advisory committee of residents, businesses, nonprofits, and farmers to guide the city’s food waste strategy.
